content: The Atlas Orthogonal Chiropractic Technique is a specialized branch of upper cervical chiropractic care. This approach emphasizes the critical role of the spine, particularly the upper cervical region, in influencing overall health. It employs precise, focused forces to correct misalignments in the spine and neck. Historically, chiropractic care initially concentrated on the upper neck, specifically the base of the skull, as correcting misalignments in this area was believed to normalize muscle tone and alleviate various conditions associated with discomfort or disease. This focus became known as Upper Cervical Specific Chiropractic. Dr. Dan Murphy, DC, DABCO, noted that over the past century, chiropractic practice has diversified into numerous specialty techniques. However, from the 1930s to the 1960s, the predominant focus of chiropractic care was on the upper cervical spine. The reasons for the decline in emphasis on upper cervical techniques remain debated. Some suggest that the philosophical and dynamic probing initiated by B.J. Palmer, a pioneer in chiropractic, has been overshadowed by followers who elevated his persona over his message. While some of Palmer's ideas may have been incorrect, they paved the way for more widely accepted methodologies, such as mobilization and therapeutic manipulation, which do not rely on philosophical or quasi-religious themes like innate intelligence or vitalism. These concepts, while significant, differ from the practical and theoretical aspects of adjusting the occipito-atlanto-axial joint complex, which this article explores. The scientific basis for the claim that the C1 vertebra (atlas) is the most influential area of the skeletal system and the most challenging to apply specific force to is still under investigation. Clinically, atlas adjustments have shown reliable results for neck pain syndromes. However, research on their efficacy for other diseases and syndromes is limited. In the realm of neuromusculoskeletal conditions, pharmacological treatments often have limited effectiveness, which is why chiropractic and other physical therapies continue to thrive despite opposition from some medical circles. The Atlas Orthogonal (AO) Chiropractic Technique is a specialty technique that focuses on adjusting the atlas vertebra and studying its relationship to human anatomy and health. This technique is rooted in the pioneering work of Dr. B.J. Palmer and later refined by Dr. John Grostic. AO is considered a whole-body technique because it views the atlas as a biomechanical and neurological keystone of body function. Palmer once emphasized the importance of the upper cervical vertebrae, stating that no other area of the body is as critical for restoring health. While chiropractors have moved away from Palmer's assertion that the upper cervical area is the cause of all diseases, there remains a lack of research into upper cervical chiropractic. Many chiropractic teaching institutions exclude upper cervical-specific techniques from their curricula, possibly to distance themselves from early fundamentalist views. The AO program, however, recognizes the importance of collaboration with other healing arts and chiropractic techniques. Referrals are made promptly if a patient does not improve within a reasonable number of visits, and AO practitioners generally oppose extended treatment plans unless they benefit the patient. The history of upper cervical chiropractic dates back to 1909 when B.J. Palmer introduced spinography at the Palmer School in Davenport, Iowa. This imaging technique remains a valuable tool for assessing adjustment vectors with accuracy and reliability. Dr. John F. Grostic, inspired by his own successful chiropractic treatment, graduated as a chiropractor in 1933 and modified Palmer's hole-in-one approach to include a more quantifiable listing of vectors. Dr. Roy Sweat, the developer of the AO technique, began his chiropractic studies in 1947 and specialized in the upper cervical occipital-atlanto-axial complex under Dr. Grostic. After Grostic's death in 1964, Dr. Sweat and others continued to advance upper cervical chiropractic through seminars and educational programs. In 1981, Dr. Sweat established the AO program, which is now taught as an elective course at several chiropractic colleges and as a postgraduate course. Dr. Sweat also developed a chiropractic adjusting instrument to deliver precise adjustments without relying on manual skills. This innovation allows new graduates to perform adjustments with consistent quality. He has designed various tools, including an atlas orthogonal x-ray frame, x-ray chair, and computerized x-ray analysis program, to enhance the accuracy of upper cervical chiropractic care. The upper cervical spine's unique anatomy and biomechanics raise specific questions about its adjustment. For example, why is so much rotation used in adjustments when the standard range of motion is only about 5 degrees? How much force is required to move such a complex joint? These questions highlight the importance of anatomical knowledge, which is a cornerstone of the AO program. B.J. Palmer emphasized the value of understanding normal osteology to appreciate the significance of the upper cervical area. The AO protocol relies on palpatory skills to detect suboccipital pain points, myofascial trigger points, and hypertonicity. Pain point tenderness has shown acceptable inter-examiner reliability. The AO practitioner assesses tissue compliance, inflammation, and tenderness at specific points corresponding to the exit of the C1 and C2 spinal nerves. These findings, combined with leg length checks, x-ray listings, clinical data, and patient history, guide the need for adjustment. The occipital-atlanto-axial joint is the most complex articulation in the axial skeleton. The mechanism by which adjustments specifically move the atlas and influence diverse clinical conditions remains controversial. However, credible hypotheses based on widely accepted facts and theories can explain the clinical outcomes of upper cervical adjustments. For instance, the cervical spine is a rich source of proprioceptive vestibular input, and dysfunction in this area may affect vestibular and visceral functions. Research on animals suggests connections between upper cervical proprioceptors and the autonomic nervous system, which may influence postural control, somatic mechanoreceptors, visual reflexes, and visceral autonomics. Connections between the cervical spine and the periaqueductal gray (PAG) have been observed in animal studies. The PAG plays a role in pain regulation and motor activities, such as vocalization and neck movements. The strongest PAG-spinal connections are found in the upper cervical cord. Mechanoreceptors in the intervertebral disc and facet joint ligaments provide critical input to the central nervous system about spinal alignment and position, influencing posture. Cervical spine dysfunction may also affect the autonomic nervous system through postural influences. Dural connections between the rectus capitis posterior minor muscle and the spinal cord's dura mater have been observed in human cadavers. Additionally, the trigeminal cervical nucleus, which extends to C4, may explain the relationship between upper cervical dysfunction and cervicogenic headaches. Abnormalities in joint end-play and position, as seen on radiographs, can contribute to cervicogenic headaches. Despite limited research, upper cervical chiropractic techniques like AO have a century of clinical results and consumer choice supporting their efficacy. Renewed interest in upper cervical care is evident, driven by patient experiences shared online, endorsements in medical literature, and research compendia for chiropractors and clinicians. The general public is encouraged to approach chiropractic care with the same scientific scrutiny as any medical procedure, considering efficacy, professional regulations, risks, and alternative options. In summary, the upper cervical area is vital to health due to its complex articulation, direct communication with the vestibular system, potential muscular connections to the spinal cord, and significant input to the thalamus and periaqueductal gray. Its unique anatomy and biomechanics make it a critical area for chiropractic care, despite being underrepresented in mainstream medical literature.
